Minerals Engineering

Volume 179, 30 March 2022, 107430

A review of environmental aspect of rare earth element extraction processes and solution purification techniques

Author links open overlay panel,
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mineng.2022.107430Get rights and content
Full text access

Highlights

  • •
    Various aspects of rare earth elements were compiled from a global perspective.
  • •
    New research initiatives and resource exploration on rare earths were investigated.
  • •
    The environmental impact of rare earth element extraction was reviewed.
  • •
    Regulatory approaches for radioactivity issues and waste disposal were addressed.
  • •
    Separation processes for thorium, uranium and rare earth elements were reviewed.

Abstract

Rare earth elements (REEs) are vital for the technology, military, and defense industries. They have been recognized as critical due to potential scarcity, supply constraints, and lack of minable concentrations. Therefore, alternative sources are needed to meet the demand and continue manufacturing rare earth-dependent products. However, the environmental prospect of rare earth mining was not investigated enough, and comprehensive studies are lacking. It demands serious consideration as toxic radionuclides are seen in the same mineralization as rare earths regardless of their primary or secondary sources. The concentration of these hazardous trace elements may be elevated as a result of extraction and beneficiation processes. Unless proper separation and disposal are performed, these radionuclides accumulate on the surface of the soil or integrate with aquatic systems, which consequently raise environmental and health concerns. This review manuscript compiled the environmental impact and aspect of rare earth extraction processes while addressing separation techniques for these radioactive materials from rare earths, emphasizing selective precipitation, solvent extraction, and solid-phase separation.

1. Introduction

Rare earth elements or lanthanides refer to 15 elements with atomic numbers from 57 to 71. Two other elements, scandium (Sc, atomic number 27) and yttrium (Y, atomic number 39) are also considered in the same group since they share similar chemical and physical properties (Rim et al., 2013, Jorjani and Shahbazi, 2016, Anderson et al., 2017, Zhou et al., 2018). Contrary to their names, the abundance of rare earths in the earth’s crust is much higher than most other commodities (Jordens, 2016, Van Gosen et al., 2017). Even the least abundant thulium and lutetium have an average crystal abundance of approximately 200 times that of gold. As opposed to thulium and lutetium, cerium, yttrium, lanthanum, and neodymium are the most abundant rare earths. On the basis of the atomic weight, rare earths are divided into two groups. The elements from lanthanum through gadolinium comprise the light rare earth elements (LREEs). In contrast, the rest and yttrium form heavy rare earths (HREEs), which are in higher demand because of their superior strategic value (Van Gosen et al., 2019). Additionally, due to their importance in many industries and shortage in supply, neodymium (Nd), terbium (Tb), yttrium (Y), dysprosium (Dy), and europium (Eu)) were classified as critical rare earth elements (CREEs) (Chu, 2011, Quinn et al., 2015).
The formation of rare earths is diverse and complex. They do not occur as native elemental metals; instead, they are seen in various host minerals, such as halides, carbonates, oxides, phosphates, and silicates (Rim et al., 2013, Suli et al., 2017). Due to the similarities in their ionic radii, the rare earths can interchange with other minerals, making their concentration difficult (Yang, 2019). Besides, concentrated rare earth deposits are limited, accounting for ineffective and uneconomical extraction (Fouquet and Martel-Jantin, 2014; McLallan et al., 2014). Although >200 rare earth-bearing minerals are being identified in nature, bastnaesite (REECO3F), monazite ((Th, REE)PO4), xenotime (REEPO4), and ion-adsorption clays are considered as the primary sources due to their rare earth contents and economic feasibility.
World resources are primarily constituted of bastnaesite and monazite deposits. Two of the world’s largest rare earth deposits, Mountain Pass (USA) and Bayan Obo (China), have bastnaesite as their rare earth host mineral, which is particularly rich in light rare earths. Monazite is generally seen in sediments and recovered, especially in coastal deposits. The deposits in Australia, Brazil, China, India, Malaysia, and South Africa constitute the largest monazite deposits. Currently, it is extracted on the east coast of Brazil and India (Van Gosen et al., 2017). Oppositely, xenotime contains a high concentration of heavy rare earths and yttrium (Alex et al., 1998). Like xenotime, ion adsorption clays also contain a considerable amount of heavy rare earths (typically 300 ppm). They are different than the mineral-type (i.e., bastnaesite, monazite, and xenotime) deposits and were discovered in granite weathering crust in Southern China in the late 60 s (Wang et al., 2018). Some of the most well-known and vital rare earth-bearing minerals are summarized in Table 1.

Because of their unique magnetic, optical, and electrical properties, rare earth elements have diverse industrial applications. As seen in Table 2, the utilization areas of rare earth elements can be grouped into three: clean energy, defense, and high-tech and daily life devices (Jyothi et al., 2020). The military uses rare earths to produce night-vision goggles, communication, and GPS equipment. Likewise, these elements are used in developing defense systems, such as jet engines, missile guidance systems, and satellites (Van Gosen et al., 2019). In addition, they are heavily used to produce electronic devices such as computers, cell phones, electric vehicle batteries, etc. Furthermore, lanthanum-based and cerium-based catalysts are commonly used in petroleum and automotive industries, whereas cerium oxide, lanthanum, and lutetium are widely used in the glass industry to provide polishing color and unique optical properties (Van Gosen et al., 2017). Producing permanent magnets from rare earth alloys is an expanding area. Neodymium is used to produce neodymium-iron-boron magnets, the strongest type of magnet (Uda et al., 2000). These magnets are used to manufacture hard disk drives, speakers, air conditioning compressors, electric motor production for hybrid cars and wind turbines (Omodara et al., 2019). Moreover, gadolinium phosphorous is used for X-ray imaging and medical applications such as MRI. Yttrium, lanthanum, and praseodymium are used as pigments for ceramics (Akdogan and Ghosh, 2014).

Even though the market prices dropped as a result of source diversification, the industrial demand is still expected to increase due to the expanded area of use and continuous growth in population and technological use (Guyonnet et al., 2015). Within that context, research and development studies have gained tremendous significance. There have been studies validating the technical feasibility of coal and coal byproducts as alternative sources for rare earth elements (Akdogan and Ghosh, 2014, Hower et al., 2016, Kolker et al., 2017, Das et al., 2018, Huang et al., 2018, Lanzerstorfer, 2018, Lin et al., 2018, Valentim et al., 2019), in which the rare earth concentrations vary between 270 and 1,480 ppm (Blissett et al., 2014, Das et al., 2018) with an average of 69 ppm on a whole mass basis (Eskanazy, 1987, Karayigit et al., 2000, Hu et al., 2006, Ketris and Yudovich, 2009, Wagner and Matiane, 2018, Huang et al., 2019). It was reported that the rare earths were associated with the incombustible material in coal rather than the combustible carbon material (Honaker et al., 2016). Alternatively, regardless of the source (i.e., coal, copper, pyrite, lead, zinc, gold mining, etc.), mine drainage also has considerable potential in being a source for rare earth elements (Costis et al., 2021). The concentration of rare earth elements in the acid mine drainage samples with solution acidity typically less than five can be as high as 130,000 µg/L. Due to the similarities in chemical characteristics, significant rare earth content can also be recovered from uranium mining wastes. It is especially a great source of scandium, which is the most valuable rare earth element among the group. An average of 0.2% rare earth oxide has been reported in various uranium mine tailings in Canada, where most uranium deposits are located (Costis et al., 2021). Moreover, electronic waste has shown significant potential as an alternative rare earth source. Recycling rare earths from electronic waste can significantly contribute to sustainability and environmental protection (Amato et al., 2019). According to 2016 data, 44.7 million tons of electronic waste were generated globally, which is projected to be even greater in the future (Jyothi et al., 2020). Although it is not desired to initiate new mining operations from a sustainability point of view, new operations have been started in India, Brazil, and Vietnam to produce rare earth as a byproduct of rutile and zircon production (Paulick and Machacek, 2017). Meanwhile, Russia and Malaysia began to recover rare earths from magnesia and cassiterite plants, respectively (Van Gosen et al., 2017). Furthermore, two previously operated mines, Mountain Pass in the U.S. and Mount Weld in Australia, were re-opened to increase their respective domestic rare earth production. In fact, in 2020, the value of rare earth compounds and metals imported by the U.S. decreased by almost 30% compared to 2019 (USGS, 2021). New deposits have also been identified in Canada, the United Kingdom, Estonia, Sweden, and Greenland (Suli et al., 2017). Researchers are also investigating the feasibility of using eudialyte, a heavy rare earth-rich mineral, phosphogypsum, the waste product of the phosphate rock and fertilizer industry, phosphate processing waste clays, apatite, cheralite, and loparite as secondary sources for rare earth elements (Dutta et al., 2016, Schreiber et al., 2016, Zhang et al., 2017, Eskanlou and Huang, 2021, Costis et al., 2021). Nickel-laterites of Cuba and the Dominican Republic and alluvial deposits of Greece may serve as significant reserves as well (Charalampides et al., 2015, Dutta et al., 2016). However, one of the challenges facing rare earth mining is the detectable radioactive matter that both conventional and unconventional rare earth sources contain (Dutta et al., 2016, Pillai, 2017). Some of the previously conducted review studies on the environmental assessment of rare earth processes are summarized and discussed in Table 5. However, this major issue still has not received the attention it requires except in a few studies (Anon, 2012, Sapsford et al., 2012, O'Callaghan, 2012, McLellan et al., 2014, Binnemans and Jones, 2015, Kumari et al., 2015, Pagano et al., 2015, Wang et al., 2016, Balaram, 2019, Omodara et al., 2019, Pagano et al., 2019, Su et al., 2020, Jyothi et al., 2020, Judge and Azimi, 2020, Garcia et al., 2020, Xiong et al., 2020). Therefore, the literature gap on rare earth element-associated hazards needs to be addressed in detail. This study targeted providing comprehensive information on the environmental aspect of rare earth elements extraction to address the knowledge gap. The subsequent section presents detailed information on environmental and health concerns arising from the radioactive elements in rare earth mineralization, considering the traditional and secondary sources. Regulatory stipulations were also covered in the next section. Afterward, separation techniques for removing radioactive and hazardous elements from rare earths were reviewed via centering around the three most commonly used methods, i.e., selective precipitation, solvent extraction, and solid-phase extraction.

2. Environmental impact of rare earth extraction and Regulatory stipulations

As previously indicated, rare earth mining faces challenges due to detectable radioactive matter. Both coal and traditional rare earth-bearing minerals currently processed contain a considerable amount of thorium and uranium due to isomorphic substitution. Therefore, it needs to be appropriately treated to prevent their interaction with groundwater and distribution to the air. In some cases, in addition to isomorphic substitution, uranium is also formed by epigenetic infiltration during the lignite-subbituminous stage of coalification (He, 2014, Ault et al., 2015, Findeiß, 2016, Qin et al., 2018, Kursun et al., 2018). If not regulated correctly, exposure to such elements may develop cancer risk for workers, severely damage surface vegetation, cause water pollution, and affect agricultural output.
It was reported that bastnaesite contains up to 0.3 wt% thorium dioxide and 0.09 wt% uranium dioxide. In contrast, monazite’s thorium and uranium contents can be as high as 20 wt% and 16 wt%, respectively. Similarly, xenotime may contain up to 5 wt% uranium dioxide (Van Gosen et al., 2017). In other words, concentrations of 238U and 232Th in these minerals exceed 1000 Bq/kg (Liu and Pan, 2011). The rare earth extraction processes can yield approximately 1.4 tons of radioactive waste in the form of solid, liquid, or gas for one ton of rare earth oxide (Jiabao and Jie, 2009, Survey, 2011, Navarro and Zhao, 2014, Dutta et al., 2016). For example, at the Bayan Obo Mine, the largest mine in China, rare earths are produced as a secondary product of iron ore, and the concentrations of ThO2 and U3O8 are 0.01–0.05% and 0.0005–0.002%, respectively (Liu and Pan, 2011). In that mine, typically, 200 tons of thorium dioxide sludge are produced every year from 100 thousand tons of rare earth concentrates. Also, according to an early study conducted at the same mine by Baotou Radiation and Environmental Institute, the radioactivity at the plant and in the soil was 32 and 1.7 times higher than the normal range. Typically, the uranium concentration in soil is between 0.3 and 11.7 mg/kg, and the average radioactivity of 234U is between 0.02 and 0.04 Bq/g (Abdel-Sabour, 2014). Likewise, the thorium content in the leaching pond was around 5 mg/L, while the thorium concentration in freshwater was 0.01 to 1 µg/L (Findeiß, 2016). In another study, it was reported that the radiation level in the Bayan Obo city areas was in the range of 100–150 nGy/h, which was 50% higher than the accepted value. This range later increased to 600–2000 nGy/h at mining sites (Liu and Pan, 2011). Similar high radiation activity results were reported in Wang and his coworkers’ (2016) study as well. According to the measurements made in the vicinity of the Bayan Obo mine, the 232Th activity in total suspended particulates in mining and smelting areas was 820–39 µBq/m3, and 720 µBq/m3 respectively, which is significantly higher than the world limit of 0.5 µBq/m3.
The chemical extraction of rare earths from monazite involves occupational radiation exposures in the range of 0.13–1 mSv per ton, depending on the concentration of monazite (Pillai, 2017). Other researchers studied thorium and uranium activity in a monazite mine in Spain and observed an activity range of 70–100 Bq/kg and 40–60 Bq/kg for thorium and uranium, separately (Garcia-Tenorio et al., 2018). The radioactivity and chemical characterization of Malaysian monazite processing residue was comprehensively investigated in Jaffary, and his coworkers’ (2019) study, which clearly pointed out that the radioactivity is above world permitted limits. Simalarly, Aziman and Ismail (2020) conducted a study to emphasize the high radioactivity level of water leach residue after processing monazite in Malaysia. For these reasons, countries like Australia and the United States stopped rare earth production from monazite in the early 90 s (Hedrick, 2000, Schuler et al., 2011). As an unconventional resource for rare earth production, coal also contains a significant amount of thorium and uranium either associated with elements in the coal itself or within the minerals that are part of coal formation (Cooper, 2005, Papastefanou, 2007, Department of Energy, 2017, Lange et al., 2017, Dai and Finkelman, 2018). Besides thorium and uranium, their decay products, such as radium and radon, are also present in coal-related materials, raising more severe concerns since they have approximately ten times higher radioactivity than thorium and uranium (USGS, 1997). While the daughter-nuclides decay with α- ß- and γ-radiation, thorium and uranium emit α-radiation which has more substantial radio-biological impacts due to the short travel distances of alpha radiation in the air as opposed to ß- and γ-radiation (Findeiß, 2016). Radon is especially unique among the decay daughters because it is a colorless, odorless, tasteless gas and may quickly distribute to the atmosphere. Its decay starts with 218Po, continues with 214Pb, 214Bi, and ends with 214Po. If proper ventilation is lacking, serious radioactivity problems may occur in the mine (Holden and Burchfield, 2010, Barakos et al., 2014). Moreover, many condensed elements with high volatility (i.e., As, Cd, Cu, Pb, etc.) are also present on the surface of fly ash samples (Parzentny and Rog, 2019).
The study conducted by Finkelman (1999) with approximately 7000 coal samples indicated that the average thorium and uranium concentrations in coal as 3.2 and 2.1 ppm, respectively. Another study conducted by Dai et al. (2014) also revealed a certain amount of uranium in coal samples taken from deposits in China and Russia. Arbuzov and his coworkers (2011) performed a detailed study on radioactive elements in coal and peat with >5000 samples collected in Northern Asia, specifically, Siberia, Russian Far East, Mongolia, and Kazakhstan. The average uranium and thorium contents for the studied locations changed between 0.6 and 32.8 ppm and 0.8–9.2 ppm, respectively. According to a characterization study conducted by the United States Geological Survey (1997) with approximately 2000 U.S. coal samples, the concentration of thorium and uranium has been found to mainly vary between 1 and 4 ppm, with the highest concentration value of 20 ppm being reported in some cases. It was reported that uranium organically bounds within the coal and may be associated with other minerals such as rare earth phosphates (Finkelman et al., 2018).
Even though the initial concentration of thorium and uranium in coal and coal byproducts is not high compared to their existence in traditional rare earth minerals, the radioactive elements can be substantially enriched along with the processing stages and may present in the solid, liquid, or gaseous wastes. The decay products or heavy metals may be released during earlier stages, such as blasting, crushing, and grinding steps, and can cause lung cancer (Findeiß, 2016). Moreover, the radionuclides may accumulate in the upper layer of the soils, form complexes with organics, and be moved into water streams or air (Abdel-Sabour, 2014). Complexes of these radioactive matter become more soluble under acidic conditions, and they may be transported through soil and plants and enter the food chain. When these toxic ions enter living organisms, such as the human body, they accumulate in the liver, spleen, and marrow, precipitating their hydroxide forms (Metaxas et al., 2003). Therefore, dust minimization and well indoor ventilation have extreme importance. It was stated that when coal is burned into fly ash, it creates a concentrated form of thorium and uranium with a concentration approximately ten times higher than the initial level (Hvistendahl, 2007). Although the direct toxicity of thorium is low because of its stability under ambient temperature, the fine thorium powder is self-ignitable (Metaxas et al., 2003). It is noteworthy that acid mine drainage (AMD) sludge has low concentrations of thorium and uranium (Vass et al., 2019). Vass et al. (2019) studied several AMD sludge samples and reported an average of 5.67 and 4.46 ppm thorium and uranium concentration, respectively. Parzentny and Rog (2019) performed a detailed study on the role of mineral matter in concentrating thorium and uranium in coal and combustion residues. The researchers also summarized the thorium and uranium contents of a wide variety of coal and coal-based samples worldwide (Table 8). The level of radioactivity in the solid waste generated from coal processing is also given in Table 9.
