In terms of regulatory approaches, various standards and rules need to be followed to dispose of these radioactive wastes or control and prevent their exposure depending on the mine source (i.e., uranium mine or rare earth mine, etc.). When naturally occurring radioactive materials are concentrated or released by human activities (i.e., mining), they are classified as technologically enhanced naturally occurring materials (TENORM) (Findeiß, 2016). The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has specific guidelines for these materials used by many countries. For example, as sustainable and cleaner production becomes more stringent in recent years, China started implementing stricter standards to develop environmentally favorable industrial practices (Wang et al., 2017). The IAEA’s safety standards were begun to be followed as a national standard for rare earth mining in 2003 to prevent ionizing radiation (Liu and Pan, 2011). Again in China, an environmental impact assessment approved by Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is requested at non-uranium mining sites containing natural radioactive nuclides. Similarly, improved effluent treatment processes are applied in India, and the radionuclide concentration in the river close to a mine site is subsequently reduced. On the other hand, in Malaysia, two rare earth processing plants were closed due to the issue of disposing of a vast amount of naturally occurring radioactive material wastes (Al-Areqi et al., 2016).
For thorium and uranium, radioactivity with less than 1 Bq/g is considered nonradioactive in every process material, and the waste is classified as exempt waste. This limit is valid for all thorium and uranium decay products (Haridasan, 2013). On the other hand, the NORM exposure limit occurring due to uranium and rare earth mining is set as 1 mSv/year for gamma exposure and 10 mSv/year for radon inhalation (IAEA, 2013). Although some of the uranium mines may have higher radon concentrations, in general, the radon concentrations are less than 100 Bq/m3, and typically, the NORM exposure occurring due to the processing of other materials is less than 1 mSv. Moreover, radioactive materials with less than 50 ppm of uranium and thorium or any combination of the two are regarded as not radioactive by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Additionally, according to the World Health Organization, the maximum uranium level in drinking water can not exceed 15 µg/L, and the maximum contaminant level set by the Environmental Protection Agency is 20 µg/L (Rozmaric et al., 2009, Camacho et al., 2010). According to the Canadian Soil Quality Guidelines, the maximum allowable concentrations of these hazardous elements are 23 ppm for agricultural and residential land use, 33 ppm for commercial land use, and 300 ppm for industrial land use. (Abdel-Sabour, 2014).
In rare earth mining sites, thorium and uranium-containing leaching wastes are generally neutralized with limestone before their disposal. If the radionuclide-containing waste is in the form of a solid, it must be kept wet by sprinkling the stockpiles to minimize dust formation. Additionally, impoundment facilities are built with waterproof materials like high-density polyethylene (HDPE) to prevent interference with soil and groundwater where the radioactive element containing tailings of rare earth mining are mixed with barium hydroxide ([BaOH]2) to precipitate those elements (Findeiß, 2016). The Australian company Lynas stores their thorium-containing waste solutions generated from the water leach process in ponds lined with HDPE. Another consideration is reducing the concentration of radioactive materials to less than 500 ppm, which is the internationally maximum allowed concentration limit to dispose of the waste without restriction. One way to do that is by mixing radioactive waste with other residues to lower the concentrations of thorium and uranium (Findeiß, 2016). At Mountain Pass mine, this procedure is followed, and the regular mining and milling tailings are co-disposed with radioactive wastes.
Separated thorium and uranium have significant potential to be used in the fuel cycle or electricity production by nuclear energy. The U.S. Department of Energy estimates an approximately 28% increase in the need for electrical power from 2012 to 2040 (Nandanwar et al., 2016). According to 2015 data, 87,000 tons (174 million pounds) of uranium (in the form of U3O8) was used in nuclear power plants worldwide, and a continuous increase is projected (Kim et al., 2016). The depleting uranium sources create a need for substitutes (Udayakumar et al., 2021). Aziman and Ismail (2020) have a thorough review study in which they investigated the sustainable recovery of thorium from the water leach residue of rare earth processing. Thorium has three to five times more potential reserves than uranium, and 232Th can be converted to 233U by absorbing slow neutrons (Kursun et al., 2018, Salehuddin et al., 2019). By converting thorium to uranium, thorium can effectively replace uranium-based nuclear reactors and become an alternative to uranium sources (Xiong et al., 2020). Therefore, if the standards are met, thorium and uranium separated from rare earth elements can create an additional production source.

3. Solution purification techniques to remove thorium and uranium from rare earth elements

The enrichment of rare earth elements requires a complex and detailed processing scheme. In general, hydrometallurgical processing techniques with various chemical compounds are applied. Typically, bastnaesite and monazite are first subjected to sample preparation and pre-concentration, including size reduction, roasting, froth flotation, which are later followed by dissolution with a strong acid (Yang et al., 2020). Physical and chemical methods to recover rare earths are well documented (Ozbayoglu and Atalay, 2000, Kim and Osseo-Asare, 2012, Jordens, 2016, Anderson et al., 2017, Suli et al., 2017, Zhang and Honaker, 2018, Honaker et al., 2019, Zhang and Honaker, 2019). However, as described earlier, thorium and uranium are also enriched alongside rare earths. Especially after leaching rare earths with acids, such as sulfuric acid (H2SO4), hydrochloric acid (HCl), or nitric acid (HNO3), these hazardous elements also dissolve, which in return, requires further purification of the leachate. Although many remediation solutions are known, only a few are feasible for a large-scale operation. This review manuscript focused on precipitation, solvent extraction, and ion exchange-adsorption processes since they are the most widely used techniques for removing radioactive elements from rare earths (Flett, 1992, Chellam and Clifford, 2002, Akkaya, 2013, Zhang and Zhao, 2016).

3.1. Selective precipitation

Selective precipitation of elements by controlled pH is the most well-known method for removing impurities from leach liquors. Besides, it has advantages of being a cost-effective and straightforward operation to perform and manage (Monhemius, 1977, Zhou et al., 2018). The underlying mechanism of precipitation is reacting chemicals with ions to generate insoluble complexes, which can then be separated from aqueous solutions by filtration (Zhou et al., 2018). Precipitation is induced by complexation using hydroxides or sulfides (Hostetler and Garrels, 1962). In the case of rare earth purification, it takes advantage of different precipitation pH ranges for thorium, uranium, and rare earths (Vijayalakshmi et al., 2001, Silva et al., 2018).
In Kim and Osseo, 2012 study, it was stated that the dissolved species of thorium, uranium, and rare earth metals in acidic solutions might be separated by pH adjustment in which thorium separation is expected to take place first. This also agrees with other literature indicating different precipitation pH ranges for thorium, uranium, and rare earths. Zhu et al. (2015) carried out a detailed review to address the environmental impact and association of thorium and uranium. As indicated in the study, in chloride media, thorium’s precipitation pH range is typically 2.5–5.5; following this, uranium and rare earth precipitations subsequently take place. The precipitation pH range of uranium and rare earths is approximately 5.5–7 and 6.8–8, respectively (Langmuir, 1978, Zhu et al., 2015). On the other hand, a shift in the precipitation pH ranges is expected when the solution medium changes. While in sulfide medium, precipitation of these elements occurs at lower pH values, in nitrate medium, insoluble complexes are formed at slightly higher pH values than chloride medium (Zhu et al., 2015, Garcia et al., 2020). However, variations may be seen depending on the elemental composition of the solutions and the concentration of the precipitation reagent used.
Thorium, with its only oxidation state, 4+, is relatively easy to work with compared to other actinide elements, such as uranium, because of the simplicity of the species (Torapava et al., 2009). Th4+ is also the largest tetravalent cation with a radius of approximately 1 Å. On the other hand, uranium can be seen in many forms (i.e., U (III, IV, V, VI)) and form various complexes such as oxides, phosphates, carbonates, etc. (Navrotsky et al., 2013). Uranium (IV and VI) are the most common and stable states (Monji et al., 2016). While U(VI) occurs in oxidizing conditions, it is seen in the form of U(IV) in reducing conditions (O'Callaghan, 2012). Chemical reactions governing the precipitation behavior of REEs3+, Th4+, and U6+ are given below (Silva et al., 2018). While most of the rare earths are usually in the form of trivalent cations, some of them may have divalent or tetravalent states as well (Charalampides et al., 2015).(1)REEs(aq)3++3OH(aq)-→REEs(OH)3(s)(2)Th(aq)4++4OH(aq)-→ThO2(s)+2H2O(3)UO2(aq)2++2OH(aq)-→UO2(OH)2(s)
A recent experimental study conducted by Talan and Huang (2020) produced coherent results with the literature. Around pH 4.8, 100% of the thorium content in a highly acidic (6 mol/L HCl) solution precipitated using 2 mol/L sodium hydroxide (NaOH), and no thorium content was detected in the remaining solution. A further increase in the pH resulted in a significant amount of rare earth element and uranium co-precipitation, >30% and 95%, respectively. The observed phenomena can be attributed to the fact that the precipitation pH range of uranium (i.e., 5.5–7) and rare earths (i.e., 6.8–8.0) overlaps to some degree, which leads to the co-precipitation of the two. Similar results were obtained when magnesium oxide and lime were used as the neutralizing agent. Mackowski et al. (2011) achieved thorium precipitation and minimal rare earth co-precipitation from a monazite sample using lime at pH 2.5. In Zhu et al. (2006) and Krebs and Furfaro’s (2013) studies, 98% and 100% thorium precipitation were seen at pH 4 and 4.8 in sulfide and chloride media, respectively. Krebs et al. (2013) study also observed almost 72% of uranium precipitation at pH 4.8. However, while Krebs and Furfaro used conventional rare earth minerals as the feedstock, Talan and Huang’s study was conducted with coarse coal refuse, leading to the difference observed in uranium precipitation. Besides, in Talan and Huang’s study, no substantial difference was observed in the precipitation recovery of thorium, uranium, and rare earths when three alkaline precipitation reagents (i.e., sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, and ammonia) were used. In another study, Al-Areqi et al., 2016 studied selective precipitation of thorium from sulfuric acid digested (H2SO4 at > 200 °C) Malaysian monazite sample using 13.4 mol/L ammonia. At pH 1.08 to 1.89, Al-Areqi and his coworkers achieved 98% thorium separation. Differently, Silva et al. (2019) used calcium carbonate to adjust the pH and precipitated thorium from sulfate solutions. In this study, in addition to thorium separation, high uranium precipitation (approximately 65%) was also achieved by increasing the solution pH to a value of 5.
On a larger scale, at the Bayan Obo Mine, the high iron content is separated at the magnetic separation step. The remaining tailings are sent to the rare earth element concentration circuit, where the rare earth elements are beneficiated using a combination of physical and chemical processes. Following froth flotation, the ore is roasted then treated with leaching. Hydrochloric acid is used to dissolve both rare earths and thorium; later, the rare earth-chloride-containing solution is transferred to a multistage solvent extraction circuit for individual separation (Schreiber et al., 2021). In China’s second-largest rare earth mine, Sichuan Mine, the ore is roasted at a temperature > 500 °C, where thorium and cerium are converted to ThO2 and CeO2. The ore is then dissolved using hydrochloric acid, where ThO2 and CeO2 remain in the leach residue while the other rare earths are selectively leached to the solution. Later, caustic attack and hydrochloric acid leaching are applied to further separate thorium from cerium (Zhu et al., 2015). At Mountain Pass Mine, bastnaesite is leached with dilute hydrochloric acid, which also dissolves uranium along with rare earths. The dissolved uranium is then selectively precipitated using barium chloride or sodium sulfate (Findeiß, 2016). Another example for separation by precipitation is the Alwaye Project in India, where the ore is leached with hydrochloric acid, later thorium is precipitated using sulfuric acid in the form of sulfate, and the rest of the solution contains rare earth elements and uranium.
In addition to the typical precipitation method of adjusting the solution pH, oxalic acid has been frequently employed to initially co-precipitate thorium and rare earths to separate them from uranium. The precipitate is subsequently subjected to selective dissolution to further separate thorium from rare earths using a hot sodium carbonate solution. Amer et al. (2013) followed this process in which alkali breakdown of monazite was first achieved and followed by dissolution-oxalate precipitation to leave uranium in the solution (Fig. 1). The solution used throughout the study was prepared using sulfuric acid with a solid to liquid ratio of 1:1.5 at 85 °C. After treatment with 30% oxalic acid at elevated temperature (60 °C) at pH 0.7, the precipitation efficiencies of rare earths and thorium reached 99%. Oxalate precipitation reactions of rare earth elements, thorium, and uranium in sulfate media are given in the reactions (4)–(7). Later, thorium separation can be achieved by dissolving the precipitated solid in a carbonate-containing solution (i.e., Na2CO3 and NaHCO3) at 75 °C, where thorium will create a soluble complex according to the reaction (8), and the rare earths will stay as insoluble. A similar use of carbonate compounds was also stated in another study where Na2CO3 was applied to wash the rare earth carbonates at 20 °C, which originated from a sulfate leach solution. By this method, approximately 98% of thorium was redissolved back into the solution and successfully separated from the rare earth elements (Zhu et al., 2015).(4)REE2(SO4)3+3H2C2O4→REE2(C2O4)3(s)+3H2SO4(5)Th(SO4)2+2H2C2O4→Th(C2O4)2(s)+2H2SO4(6)UO2(SO4)+H2C2O4→UO2(C2O4)(s)+H2SO4(7)UO2C2O4+3H2SO4→UO2SO4(s)+2CO2+3H2O(8)Th(C2O2)2(s)+4Na2CO3+2NaHCO3→Na6Th(CO3)5+2Na2C2O4(s)+H2O+CO2
Double salt precipitation with sodium or sulfate is an alternative method frequently used in the United States and China; however, this method is typically employed to separate cerium from the rest of the trivalent rare earth elements. Although some studies report thorium precipitation as high as 80%, other studies state lower thorium precipitation (25–30%) (Zhu et al., 2015). Meantime, thorium’s ability to form double salts is limited, but it can be co-precipitated and then further separated. In the case of uranium, the co-precipitation depends on uranium’s nature in solution. If uranium is in the form of U(VI), its co-precipitation is even lower than what is observed for thorium. On the other hand, if it is in the form of U(IV), its co-precipitation with cerium can be very high. Therefore, this method varies depending on the operational conditions and ore characteristics. The chemical reaction representing the rare earth double salt precipitation is given in reaction (9).(9)M++RE3++2SO42-+XH2O→MRE((SO)4)2.XH2O
where the single valence M+ ion can be NH4+, K+, or Na+. Arafura Resources of Australia utilized this process to separate uranium from rare earths with double salt precipitation (Na2SO4), where uranium stays in the solution. It is targeted to leave a portion of thorium into the solution, where it can be further removed from uranium via precipitation if required. The amount of thorium precipitated together with rare earths during double salt precipitation can be subjected to redissolution with a concentrated hydrochloric acid solution at pH 1–1.5 and neutralize with a basic solution at pH 4–5 to selectively remove thorium from rare earth elements (Lockyer, 2014, Zhu et al., 2015). The schematic representation of the process is given in Fig. 2.

3.2. Solvent extraction

Solvent extraction has been the most extensively used method for solution purification due to its ability to handle large volumes of aqueous solutions (Asselin et al., 1949, Hidayah and Abidin, 2017). It has also been an effective technique to remove hazardous matters from rare earths (Brown and Sherrington, 1979).
One of the crucial parameters in the solvent extraction process is the type and concentration of the extractant (organic chemical) since the efficiency of the procedure depends significantly on the extractant’s ability to transfer metal ions between two immiscible phases; aqueous and organic (Hidayah and Abidin, 2017, Zhou et al., 2018). Organic phosphorus acid, carboxylic acid, tertiary and quaternary amines, and sulphoxide are some of the commercially used extractant types, which have been proved to be effective for the separation of radioactive elements while present with rare earths (Palmieri, 1987, Gupta et al., 2002, Belova et al., 2015, Zhu et al., 2015, Giri and Nath, 2016, Kuang et al., 2017). However, most of these extractants are also effective for recovering rare earths. Therefore, developing a unique experimental scheme for the desired selectivity and separation efficiency is crucial.
Many studies have been conducted to investigate the impact of different extractant types, diluents, and operating conditions on removing thorium and uranium from traditional rare earth-bearing minerals (Nasab, 2014, Samsonov et al., 2015, Lu et al., 2016, Wang et al., 2017). One of the earliest studies in this field was conducted by Hughes and Singh (1980), who used a secondary amine (Adogen 283) to separate thorium from monazite and achieved a thorium dioxide grade of >99% from the strip solution. On the other hand, Amaral and Morais (2010) studied the removal of thorium and uranium from sulfuric leach liquor generated from monazite leaching using a mixture of primary and tertiary amine (Primene JM-T and Alamine 336) extractants to observe the synergetic extraction. A combination of primary and tertiary amines at one step can help the mutual separation of thorium and uranium and contribute to the economic aspect of extraction circuits by reducing the number of steps required. During their study, high extraction recoveries were obtained for thorium and uranium (>99% for both) while co-extracting only 0.1% of the rare earth elements. The expected reactions between primary amine and thorium and tertiary amine and uranium are separately given in reactions (10), (11). These two reactions are also the foundation of the AMEX process developed in the 1950 s to remove thorium and uranium from rare earth elements in sulfate leachate. Following the extraction of thorium via primary extractants, nitric acid is used as the strippant. Differently, for uranium, sodium carbonate is used as the stripping agent (Garcia et al., 2020). Although Hughes and Singh (1980) stated more thorium and uranium introduction to the system is inevitable when primary amines were used to prevent the co-extraction of the lanthanides, Amaral and Morais’ (2010) study reported a selective extraction between thorium, uranium, and rare earths when Primene JM-T and Alamine 336 were used as the extractants with significantly low rare earth co-extraction (Fig. 3).(10)4RNH2H+HSO4-+(Th(SO4)4)-→RNH2H+4(ThSO44)4-+4HSO4-(11)4R3NH+HSO4-+(UO2(SO4)3)4-→R3NH+4(UO2SO43)4-+4HSO4-
Even though tertiary amines are more preferential for uranium removal and primary amines are more selective towards thorium in sulfuric acid media (Shimidt, 1971), in Borai and his coworkers’ (2014) study, a primary amine was reported to be the most efficient one towards both thorium and uranium. While 90% of uranium extraction using 0.1 mol/L Octylamine at pH 4 was achieved, thorium extraction was higher (97%) and required lower chemical concentration (0.01 mol/L) and pH value (3). However, when the system was changed to a multielement system, tertiary amines were more favorable for the extraction of thorium and uranium. As a result, 80% of thorium separation was achieved using 0.01 mol/L N,N-dimethyl aniline at pH 4. On the other hand, 66% of uranium removal was reported using 0.1 mol/L extractant at pH 7 (Borai et al., 2014).
Another type of extractants commonly used are acid organophosphorus, including Cyanex series, di-(2-Ethylhexyl)-phosphoric acid (DEHP), (2-Ethylhexyl) 2-Ethylhexyl-phosphonic acid (EHEHP), and di-(2-Ethylhexyl) 2-Ethylhexyl phosphonate (DEHEHP) (Garcia et al., 2020). Gupta et al. (2002) investigated thorium and uranium separation from rare earths using Cyanex 923. Furthermore, Nasab et al. (2011) studied thorium removal using Cyanex 272 and Cyanex 302 as the extractants. Although good selectivity and high purity were achieved in the study conducted by Gupta et al. (2002), Nasab used the other forms of Cyanex extractants to minimize the multistage stripping for Cyanex 923. One drawback of the Cyanex series is that they require high acidity, rendering them infeasible for industrial-scale applications from an economic standpoint. The extraction of thorium and uranium with Cyanex extractants occur according to the following reactions, where R represents the extractant:(12)Th4++4NO3-+3R→Th(NO3)43R(13)UO22++2NO3-+2R→UO2(NO3)22R
Tributyl phosphate (TBP), a neutral organophosphorus extractant, is also indicated as an effective extractant for thorium and uranium separation. Extraction reactions of thorium and uranium when an organophosphorus extractant is used are given in reactions (14), (15). However, the use of TBP is restricted to the extraction from nitrate and chloride media (Gupta et al., 2002). Ordinarily, nitric acid is not preferred for leaching purposes except for nuclear waste treatment. Purification of impurities using TBP in kerosene also required multi-stage extracting and stripping (Al-Areqi et al., 2015). Multiple contacts between aqueous and organic solutions may increase the extraction efficiency; however, the organic extractant tends to be lost into the aqueous phase after a long contact between aqueous and organic phases. For example, Saskatchewan Research Council has built a pilot-scale processing plant that produces high purity (99%) rare earth via co-extraction of rare earths and uranium. The primary separation technique is based on multi-stage solvent extraction, where around 150 mixer-settlers are used. In a smaller laboratory scale, in Talan and Huang’s (2020) study, a two-stage solvent extraction process proved to be more efficient than the single-stage process, during the former method of which approximately 97%, 94%, and 43% of rare earths, thorium, and uranium were recovered into the circuit rare earth product stream, respectively.
Qi (2018) studied the extraction mechanism of thorium, uranium, and rare earths in the TBP-HCl system and stated that the extraction order is UO22+ > Th4+ > REE3+. When present with the three ion groups, TBP forms complexes with the ions in the solution according to their distinctive capabilities to bind with the extractant (Rand et al., 2008). Similarly, Nasab (2014) observed that uranium extraction is more feasible than thorium in a chloride medium, attributed to the species formed between uranium and hydrochloride that TBP readily extracts by forming soluble organic complexes. On the other hand, thorium purification by solvent extraction in nitric acid media is more favorable over rare earth elements (Menzies and Rigby, 1961, Al-Areqi et al., 2014). Nitrate is a preferred medium for enhanced extraction of thorium due to an associated increase in the hydration energy of the anions (Nasab, 2014, Lu et al., 2016).
Tris(2-Ethylhexyl) phosphate (TEHP) and tri-iso-amyl phosphate (TiAP) are other neutral organophosphorus extractants, which are typically dissolved in n-paraffin or xylene, as opposed to kerosene. Biswas et al. (2013) performed a comparative study to remove thorium and uranium from a monazite sample using TBP and TEHP. The process flowsheet followed during their research is given in Fig. 4. Hot alkali digestion of monazite occurs, followed by washing with water to separate thorium, uranium, and rare earth elements as their hydroxide form. Later, selective dissolution of rare earth elements is targeted using hydrochloric acid at pH 3, where thorium, uranium, and a portion of rare earths stayed as insoluble compounds and later dissolved separately using 2–3 mol/L nitric acid. Subsequently, solvent extraction steps were employed, and>99% of uranium was separated using 0.2 mol/L TEHP in a multistep circuit.(14)UO22++2NO3-+2X→UO2(NO3)2.2X(15)Th4++4NO3-+3X→Th(NO3)4.3X
When the extraction is completed, the extractant is stripped by mixing the solution with acids. This step removes ions from the organic phase, draws them into the aqueous acids, and regenerates the extractant (Jorjani and Shahbazi, 2016). Talan and Huang (2020) examined the difference between DI water and sulfuric acid in stripping efficiency. They stated that the stripping agent is not a significant parameter on the separation of uranium from rare earth aqueous solution, at least for the studied two solutions. In the researchers’ study, the lowest uranium recovery of 1.8 wt% into the final rare earth product stream was achieved under the conditions of 50 v% TBP, feed pH at 3.5, organic to aqueous phase ratio at 3, and 1 mol/L sulfuric acid as the strippant. Similarly, Biswas et al. (2013) used water to strip uranium-loaded extractant phase and achieved good recovery (>99%) in three stripping stages with the organic to aqueous phase ratio of 1:1. In some cases, a combination of two processes can be applied. The flowsheet seen in Fig. 5 shows the separation process employed by the Kvenfjeld project in Greenland. It is an example where two techniques are used to separate thorium and uranium from the rare earth elements. As seen, while uranium is separated via solvent extraction, thorium is removed in the subsequent steps via hydrochloric acid leaching.
Nonetheless, these separation processes may result in the loss of rare earths into impurity residues to a certain degree. For example, during the impurity removal process of ion adsorbed clays, approximately 15% of rare earth elements may be lost to residues. In comparison, around 2% of it transferred to neutralization residues produced from acidic wastewater. In that aspect, Su and his coworkers (2020) developed a cost-effective process (Fig. 6) for recovering thorium and rare earth elements from radioactive residue that those two were co-present. Following the flowsheet, first, thorium separation via liquid–liquid extraction is targeted, followed by the combination of extraction and precipitation for further rare earth recovery. Another example of a combined approach was given in an early Eco Ridge Mine project report. After co-extraction of uranium and rare earths during the preconcentration steps, uranium is removed via solvent extraction using 2.5 v% Alamine and 2.5 v% Isodecanol mixture as the extractant. The remaining solution is then treated with an organic mixture (i.e., 10% D2EHPA and 2% TBP) and a stripping reagent (i.e., 1.5 N HNO3 mixed with 1.5 N H2SO4) to remove rare earth elements from the rest of the impurities (i.e., thorium and iron). Lastly, the stripped solution is neutralized with lime to a pH value of 3.2 to separate thorium and iron that might come to the solution (Costis et al., 2021).

3.3. Separation using Solid-Phase extraction techniques

Separation using solid materials is heavily used in metal separations, water and wastewater treatment, removal, and recovery of metal ions (Sani et al., 2015). Ion exchange and adsorption processes are two very similar solid–liquid separation techniques. However, adsorption can be explained by electrical attraction to the solid surface. In contrast, ion exchange is defined as a process in which the chemical energy at equilibrium after the process is lower than the initial (Jorgensen, 1989).

3.3.1. Ion exchange

Ion exchange is a process in which ions are exchanged between a solution and a solid (Hidayah and Abidin, 2017). The exchange reaction between ions in solution and ions attached to the matrix is generally reversible. The following reaction represents a fundamental exchange mechanism:(16)Asolution+Bsolid→Asolid+B(solution)
Before the development of solvent extraction, ion exchange was known as the most practical method to separate rare earths from impurities (Suli et al., 2017). It has also been used for fuel processing containing thorium and uranium (Chen et al., 2016). Even though the ion exchange application has been lessened, the need arises when the loss of extractant into the aqueous phase or high impurity in the final product is seen during the solvent extraction process. In addition, ion exchange requires fewer separation steps and consumes less chemical reagents compared to solvent extraction (Ferrah et al., 2011).
The resins used for the ion exchange are highly ionic reactive polymers, covalently crosslinked, and classified based on the charge of the counter ion exchanger (Bertoli et al., 2019). Anion and cation resins are the two most common types used in the ion-exchange process, which further divide into two subgroups, respectively, as strong base anionic, strong acid cationic, and weak base anionic and weak acid cationic resins. While anion resins attract negatively charged ions, cation resins attract positively charged ions. A summary of the resin types and the chemical structures is given in Table 10.

Table 10. Resin types, the functional groups, and their chemical structures (modified from Ang et al., 2017).

Resin TypeFunctional GroupChemical Structure
Strong-base anionic ion exchangerQuaternary amine type 1
Quaternary amine type 2
Weak-base anionic ion exchangerTertiary amine
Primary amine
Strong-acid cationic ion exchangerSulfonic acid
Weak-acid cationic ion exchangerCarboxylic acid
Several studies were conducted to remove radioactive elements from aqueous solutions by using various ion exchange resins (Song et al., 1999, Vaaramaa et al., 2000, Merdivan et al., 2001, Chandramouleeswaran et al., 2011, Pulhani et al., 2012, Rahmati et al., 2012, Semnani et al., 2012, Chen et al., 2016, Qiu et al., 2017, Bertoli et al., 2019). Ang and his coworkers (2017) performed a comprehensive study that examined the effectiveness of nine anionic and four cationic resins on removing thorium and uranium from rare earth elements. Resin 1 was a primary amine weak-base anion exchanger within the nine anionic exchangers, resin 2 and 3 were tertiary and quaternary amino groups containing intermediate-base anion exchanger, and resins 4 to 9 were quaternary ammonium group containing strong-base anion exchangers. On the other hand, within the four cationic resins, two of them were sulfonic acid strong acid cation exchangers, and the other two were carboxylic weak-acid cation exchangers. In Ang and his coworkers’ study, a synthetic solution containing 2 mmol/L of thorium, uranium, and rare earth elements in sulfate media was treated with various anionic exchangers for a total of 24 h contact time. The primary amine weak-base anion exchanger showed superior efficiency for thorium, while an opposite behavior was observed for uranium. Uranium exchange recoveries were higher for the other types of anionic exchange resins. The researchers concluded that rather than being weak or strong base anionic exchangers, the functional groups are more influential on the results. Overall, the weak-base anionic resin resulted in the best results with less than 5% rare earth co-exchange, while thorium and uranium separation was approximately 70% and 68% at pH 3 with 0.0005 mol/L sulfuric acid. However, in another study, when the solution medium is nitrate, thorium adsorption using strong base anionic resins have been reported to be more favorable (Judge and Azimi, 2020). The anion exchange of thorium from nitrate media is given in reaction (17). Anion exchange of uranium from sulfate media is provided in reaction (18), where X- represents the counter ion initially loaded on the resin.
On the other hand, in the case of cationic exchangers, a higher affinity towards rare earths was observed by Ang et al. (2017). The researchers did not see any significant improvement in the adsorption recovery of uranium (nearly 30%) when the contact time was increased from 2 h to 24 h. On the contrary, the adsorption of rare earths (>95%) and thorium (80%) were doubled when the contact time was increased. Uranium anionic species can explain the low uranium uptake in a cationic resin environment. Contrarily, the high affinity of strong-base cationic resins toward rare earth element and thorium is because of their higher metal charges. The best separation results were achieved when the sulfuric acid concentration was between 0.05 and 0.1 mol/L and the pH was between 0.07 and 1.(17)Th(NO3)62-+2P-NR3X→(P-NR3)2Th(NO3)6+2X-(18)UO2(SO4)34-+4P-NR3X→(P-NR3)4UO2(SO4)3+4X-
Korkisch and Tera, 1961, Gu et al., 2005, and Ladeira and Goncalves (2007) performed ion exchange studies with strong-base anion exchange resins, which are indicated as the most suitable resin type for thorium and uranium recovery, especially when they are recovered individually other than simultaneously. The effectiveness of this resin type is exceptionally superior in sulfate and nitrate media (Judge and Azimi, 2020). The strong-base anionic resins have quaternary amine (NR3+) in their functional groups to make ion exchange happen. In Gu and his coworkers’ study, all six tested resins (i.e., A530E, A500, A520E, A850, Dowex 1-X8, WBR 109) showed good affinity towards uranium with 8 to 24 h of retention time, regardless of the sulfate concentration of the solution. However, the researchers stated that Purolite A850 has the highest affinity for uranium while Dowex 1-X8 and Purolite A500 have the lowest affinity. The reason for relatively different adsorption between the resins can be due to the differences in their exchange sites. For example, while WBR109 has smaller tributyl ammonium exchange sites, A530E has larger tri hexyl ammonium sites, and DOWEX 1-X8 and A500 both have tri methyl ammonium functional groups. In general, the adsorption rate increases as the length of tri alkyl ammonium functional groups decreases. However, the researchers stated the ineffectiveness of the resins studied at high pH values. When the pH exceeds typically 4, hydrolysis of other ions is noticed, which may be sorbed by the resins and reduce the separation efficiency. Moreover, precipitation of the ions of interest may happen at higher pH values, decreasing the separation performance. For example, in Korkisch and Tera’s study (1961), it was stated that the uptake of lanthanides could be eliminated by keeping the pH at 4.5 and preventing the hydrolysis of lanthanides. On the contrary, Gu and his coworkers’ study was conducted at pH 8.5, resulting in high uranium removal.
On the other hand, Ladeira and Goncalves (2007) studied uranium removal from acid mine water at a maximum pH value of 3.9 to prevent uranium precipitation. This pH value also enhanced the uranium uptake since the accompanied iron ions precipitated as iron (III) hydroxide. The strong base anionic resins and strong acid cationic resins can be active at any pH level. However, weak acid cationic resins are more favorable due to their opposite behavior and ability to release H+, which results in higher ion exchange capacity than strong acid cation exchangers (Hidayah and Abidin, 2017), even though they act inactive in pH 4–6. Similarly, weak base anionic resins have limitations by working only at very low pH regions. Vaaramaa et al. (2000) conducted a study to compare strong-base anionic exchangers with aminophosphonate. It was reported that at pH 5, aminophosphonate resin worked better than strong-base anionic resin; however, due to the presence of UO2(SO4)3-4 type of ions, the use of strong-base anionic resins are more favorable when acidic water feedstock is used.
Ion exchange is a selective process, which means the ions attached to the matrix will prefer one counter ion over another. For instance, Semnani et al. (2012) observed that the affinity of uranium onto Amberlite CG-400 resin decreases when the phosphate anions in the solution increase since phosphate anions will compete with uranium anions. The formation of phosphate anions is due to the rise in pH, which is a vital parameter for a successful ion exchange process. Ang and his coworkers (2017) observed a similar competing behavior between uranium and sulfate ions. Sulfuric acid concentration of the medium was stated as an influential parameter when ion exchangeability was investigated, and a suppressing effect of sulfate ions was observed. Effective uranium separation was achieved when the sulfuric acid concentration was 0.1 mol/L or lower and the solution pH was > 0.7. Cheira et al. (2017) also studied uranium separation from a sulfate leach liquor by an anionic exchange resin, Ambersep 920U SO4. The researchers first observed an increase in the uranium adsorption as pH increased from 1 to 2. It reached a maximum at pH 2–3.5, which then started to decrease between pH 3.5 and 5 due to the formation of precipitates. Higher adsorption recoveries were also obtained as contact time and adsorbent amount were gradually increased from 10 to 120 mins and 25 to 200 mg, respectively. As a result, 99% of uranium adsorption was generated using 200 mg of Ambersep 920U SO4 at pH 2 with a contact time of 120 mins.
Sometimes, more than one technique is used to enhance separation efficiency. For example, Papadopoulos et al. (2004) applied both precipitation and ion exchange techniques to increase the removal rate by 20% compared to a single technique. Another group of researchers also applied a combined approach to selectively separate uranium and rare earth elements (Hamza et al., 2019). Their study first used selective precipitation to separate impurities; then, the solution was treated with a magnetic resin to separate uranium from rare earth elements. A high enrichment factor was achieved, and the final residue was uranium-depleted. Nonetheless, due to the limitations of the ion exchange feed flow rate, the application of liquid–liquid extraction processes is preferred from the standpoint of potential scale-up (Garcia et al., 2020). Moreover, it is a highly complicated phenomenon that depends significantly on the nature of the materials and the aqueous chemistry of the system.
Another group of ion exchangers is chelating and solvent-impregnated resins. Chelating resins were developed to overcome the limitations in traditional cationic and anionic ion exchangers. They exhibit higher selectivity than the conventional resins since they can undergo surface modifications, thus, making themselves more selective to the ions of interest. Impregnated resins, on the other hand, are accepted as an alternative to solvent extraction systems, and they are simply produced by reacting a solvent with insoluble support (resins). The solvent is contacted with the resin, which soaks the extractant rather than forming bonding. Page et al. (2017) studied several chelating resins, including mixed sulfonic/phosphonic, aminophosphonic, and iminodiacetic acid functional groups, to observe their ability to separate individual rare earths; however, the study indicated no significant affinity towards rare earths. Instead, it was concluded that these chelating resins could be applied to remove impurity elements, such as iron, thorium, and uranium. Ang et al. (2018) performed a detailed study where five chelating and two impregnated resins were evaluated based on their performance of removing uranium and thorium from rare earth elements in sulfate medium. Within the five tested chelating resins, the one with the bis-picolylamine group showed relatively higher affinity for uranium in 0.05 mol/L sulfuric acid at 2 h contact time. While the adsorption recovery of uranium was 44%, the recovery of rare earth elements and thorium under the same conditions was 10% and 16%, separately. The uranium adsorption increased to 89% when the contact time was increased to 24 h while keeping the acidity constant. However, this new operating condition observed no difference in the adsorption of thorium or rare earths. For simultaneous separation of thorium and uranium, iminodiacetic chelating resins yielded better performance. With 24 h contact time and 0.05 mol/L solution acidity, adsorption of uranium and thorium were around 70% and 60%, respectively. The rare earth adsorption under the same conditions was less than 8%. However, based on the tested acidity range (i.e., 0.0005 to 2 mol/L), feasible separation of thorium and uranium from rare earths was achieved when the solution acidity was 0.1 mol/L or lower, and the best separation performance was achieved when the solution medium was 0.005 mol/L sulfuric acid and at pH 2. Under these operating conditions, uranium and thorium adsorption was around 90%, while rare earth adsorption was below 30%. Nevertheless, no separation was observed between the elements when chelating resins containing the aminophosphonic functional group were used regardless of the contact time. On the other hand, between the explored impregnated resins, the highest uranium adsorption recovery of 93% was achieved with a bis-(2,4,4-trimethylpentyl) phosphinic acid impregnated resin (0.05 mol/L H2SO4, 2-hour contact). Although commonly used in commercial solvent extraction units, D2EHPA impregnated resin did not yield high adsorption. The maximum uranium adsorption was 65% generated at the end of 24 h contact time. The thorium removal was around 45%, and the rare earth adsorption recovery was around 15% under the same testing conditions.
Similarly, Reynier et al. (2021) investigated the selectivity of several resin types, including the chelating and impregnated resins, on the recovery of thorium, uranium, and rare earth elements from a bio-leached uranium tailing sample. Among the five chelating resins with different functional groups (i.e., thiol, thiourea, bis-picolylamine, aminomethyl phosphonic, iminodiacetate), Lewatit TP260 with aminomethyl phosphonic functional group resulted in better separation between thorium, uranium, and rare earth elements. The respective recovery values were reported as 55%, 93%, and 30%, respectively. Among the tested impregnated resins, D2EHPA-impregnated Lewatit VPOC 026 resulted in enhanced separation than trimethyl pentyl-phosphinic-impregnated Lewatit TP 272 resin. The former produced 69% of thorium, 71% of uranium, and approximately 20% of rare earth removal. However, both chelating and D2EHPA impregnated resins co-recovered a substantial amount of scandium, >65%. Qui et al. (2017) studied ODP impregnated resin to remove thorium and uranium from rare earth elements. 64% of thorium separation was achieved with ODP impregnated resin in nitrate media while rare earth and impurity elements (such as iron) co-extraction were minimal. The separation efficiency of thorium was increased to an even higher value of 95% when D2EHPA impregnated resin was used, and uranium separation efficiency was around 80%.

3.3.2. Adsorption

Nowadays, the application of adsorption using porous solid sorbent has been gradually increased due to its high efficiency, easy handling, low maintenance, and operating costs over other techniques (Liu et al., 2013, Nandanwar et al., 2016). It has advantages over conventionally used solvent extraction by eliminating the consumption of organic extractants and reducing environmental pollution that organic chemicals may create (Xiong et al., 2020). Adsorption has also been used for fuel processing, containing thorium and uranium (Chen et al., 2016).
Sorbents are available in various forms, such as natural and synthetic organic, inorganic, or composite materials. Their surfaces are often heterogeneous, and bonding energies may vary from one site to another. Materials like zeolite, apatite, activated carbon, calcined phosphate, oxides, and hydroxides are examples of some highly abundant sorbents (Ladeira and Goncalves, 2007). Especially silica-based materials have suitable physical, chemical, and thermal stability. There are plenty of studies about thorium and uranium adsorption on different materials (Aksoyoglu, 1989, Badei et al., 1992, Milonjic et al., 1992, Qadeer et al., 1992, Jain et al., 2001, Kilislioglu and Bilgin, 2003, Humelnicu et al., 2006, Sikalidis et al., 2008, Wang et al., 2012, Liu et al., 2013, Kaynar et al., 2015). The adsorption mechanism starts with a complex formation directly with the adsorbent surface, which lies on the Stern Layer. As the valence of a cation increases, the tendency of complexation also increases. Later the cation creates an outer-sphere complex, in which at least one water molecule is in between the cation and the adsorbent. Sometimes, the cation, which is surrounded by water molecules, may locally neutralize the surface charge of the adsorbent instead of forming a complex. In that case, the ion lies in the diffusion layer. While the complexes on the Stern layer may have covalent or ionic bonding, the ions in the diffusion layer only have ionic bonds. Following adsorption, desorption is performed by either elevating the temperature, reducing the pressure, or washing with a suitable reagent. The desorbed material may be recovered as a valuable product or discarded as waste (Couper et al., 2009).
The adsorption process depends on the chemical nature of both fluid and solid. Also, it is highly affected by the available surface area and pore volume of the adsorbent. Besides, the selectivity depends on many other factors such as the particle size of the absorbent, pH of the solution, contact time, nature of the solution, etc. The pH plays an essential role in sorption processes because it can influence the aqueous chemistry of the ions determining the hydrolysis products and the properties of the active sites of the sorbent (Faghihian et al., 2004, Cheira et al., 2017). It also affects the external charge of the adsorbent, which results in a change in the electrostatic interactions. It was seen that the capacity of uranium adsorption increases with increasing pH and reaches a maximum value at a pH range of 2.0 to 3.5 (Cheira et al., 2017). Another report published by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (1999) stated that when carbonate ions are present, the adsorption of uranium reaches its maximum in the pH range of 5 to 8 and decreases as the pH continues to increase. Osthols’ (1995) study on adsorption of thorium onto amorphous colloidal silica particles indicated that the most efficient pH range is between 3 and 6. As pH reaches neutral and alkaline values, it was observed that the silica sites are not adsorbing thorium sufficiently anymore. In general, due to the formation of hydrolysis products, the adsorption of thorium and uranium onto various adsorbents is kept below pH 5 (Sikalidis et al., 2008). Particle size distribution is another critical factor due to its influence on the pressure loss upon passing the solvent through the sorbent. It also affects mass transfer rates. Pressure loss increases with decreasing particle size, and mass exchange rates also increase with decreasing particle size because of shorter diffusion paths (Kammerer et al., 2011, Monji et al., 2016). An increase in adsorption capacity is expected when the particles are finer since the effective surface area increases as the size decreases (Zou et al., 2009). The pore size distribution also plays a significant role in the diffusion of the solutes onto the sorbents. Compounds with an amphoteric nature obtain the maximum adsorption at the isoelectric point (Jorgensen, 1989).
In the early years, Doi et al. (1975) conducted a comprehensive study about uranium adsorption on a wide variety of sorbents such as peat, ferric oxide, clay minerals, zeolite, calcite, and apatite. The highest uranium uptake on peat was observed at a pH range of 3.8–8.5. It was noticed that the humic acid in the peat was causing uranium adsorption. As the coalification progressed, uranium adsorption decreased in the order of peat, lignite, bituminous coal, and anthracite. The same researchers also studied adsorption by calcite and apatite, which resulted in a positive correlation between adsorption and the amount of sorbent used. Khalili and Al-Banna (2015) studied thorium and uranium adsorption by humic acid. They stated that adsorption by humic substances is achieved via forming complexes with carboxylic and other acidic functional groups by replacing hydrogen ions with the ions of interest. Fasfous and Dawoud (2012) performed a thorough study on uranium adsorption by multi-walled carbon nanotubes (CNT). The researchers also examined the kinetic and thermodynamic aspects of the adsorption process. CNT is more favorable among carbon-based materials (i.e., carbon nanotubes, graphene, carbon fibers) due to its high specific surface area (Yadav et al., 2019). Alternatively, Kutahyali and Eral (2010) investigated the adsorption of thorium and uranium on activated carbon. In a similar study performed with activated carbon, Yakout (2017) stated that uranium adsorption on KOH-modified activated carbon is more selective than thorium adsorption. In contrast, thorium uptake is higher on nitric acid-modified activated carbon. Monji et al., 2016, Youssef et al., 2018 studied the adsorption of uranium ions in the presence of lanthanides using a byproduct of the agricultural industry. Considering the immense quantities of agricultural waste, their use for the adsorption of ions substantially benefits the environment. Among the seven different agricultural waste types, Monji et al. reported that rice bran has higher selectivity for uranium in 4 mol/L hydrochloric acid when lanthanides are present. On the contrary, pine tree sawdust, tea factory waste, wheat bran, rice hull, orange peel, and lemon peel were found to be less effective due to competition between hydrogen and uranium ions at the binding sites.
Most recently, Xiong et al. (2020) studied membrane-based separation using a novel sorbent (covalent organic frameworks, i.e., COFs). Separation via membranes is achieved by forming a complex between the element of interest and the membrane. Adsorption via membrane is efficient in acidic conditions and at pH values between 4 and 5.5. Besides, it consumes less energy, is easy to operate, and has an increased diffusion rate, resulting in enhanced high-speed adsorption (Xu et al., 2009, Garcia et al., 2020). In Xiong and his coworkers’ study, high and fast adsorption capacities for thorium were observed at all tested pH values (1 to 2.8). The adsorption mechanism was determined as pseudo-second-order chemical adsorption. Hunter et al. (1988) studied thorium uptake by goethite and nsutite (ɤ-MnO2) and observed the formation of competitive complexes. In their study, as the concentration of sulfate ions increases, the adsorption of thorium decreases due to the competition between the two ions.
As another group of sorbents, microorganisms are frequently studied. The use of microorganisms is the cheapest and most environmentally friendly route of ion adsorption. Bacillus subtilis, Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas fluorescens, Paracoccus denitrificans, Schwanella putrefaciens, and Alcaligenes faecalis are the most common microorganisms (Hidayah and Abidin, 2017). For example, Bacillus subtilis tends to separate heavy rare earth elements in which the absorption is fast (around 10 mins) and at a relatively low pH level (i.e., 4). Although higher bacteria concentration seems favorable, a further increase in pH causes degradation and reduces the separation performance. Tsezos and Volesky (1982) studied thorium uptake by a different microorganism, Rhizopus Arrhizus, and observed optimum thorium biosorption at pH 4 by a rapid process. Bhainsa and D'Souza, 2001, Nakajima and Tsuruta, 2004 investigated uranium uptake on Systoseira Indica and reported similar results. Maximum adsorption was achieved in both studies at pH 4, around 25–30 °C, with a retention time of 3 h. Similarly, an engineered bacteria was used by Bonificio and Clarke (2016). Nonetheless, the use of microorganisms is effective on a small scale; their application on an industrial scale was stated as uneconomical (Hidayah and Abidin, 2017).
Sometimes the sorbent needs surface modification to enhance its adsorption capability. The modified material is called synthetic sorbent, which is more stable compared to its natural form (Ullah et al., 2012). Uranium removal by manganese oxide-coated and iron oxide-coated zeolite samples were studied extensively by multiple researchers (Han et al., 2007, Zou et al., 2009, Nekhunguni et al., 2017). Iron and manganese oxides are expected to be more effective than other adsorbents. Generally, an increase in the adsorption capacity was observed with an increased pH until 6 and adsorbent amount. However, compared to clinoptilolite type zeolite, magnetite nanoparticles, and titanium oxide modified clays, the adsorption capacity of iron oxide-coated zeolite samples was significantly lower in Nekhunguni and his coworkers’ (2017) study. In another study by Wang et al. (2013), a synthesized mesoporous material named SBA-15 was used to remove uranium in a nitrate medium. Consistent with previously mentioned studies, this study also reported increased uranium adsorption with an elevated pH. However, after pH 6, the uranium adsorption slowed down and diminished due to the dissolved carbonate and bicarbonate ions, which compete with the uranium ions for available adsorption sites. The study achieved 79% uranium adsorption with the synthesized adsorbent in 30 min of equilibrium time at pH 6. Kinetic adsorption studies suggested Langmuir isotherm and pseudo-second-order rate for the studied system.
On the other hand, Metaxas et al. (2003) focused on thorium adsorption using different zeolite samples in addition to investigating the effect of the modified (pretreated) samples. Metaxas and his coworkers’ study (2003) showed that NaCl-treated synthetic zeolites had higher removal efficiency than natural zeolite samples. The reason for higher removal with synthetic zeolites is their larger framework channels and their higher number of active exchange sites. On the other hand, compared to clinoptilolite type zeolite, mordenite type zeolite was more efficient. While the thorium removal with Na-mordenite was 0.64 meq/g, it was significantly lower (0.25 meq/g) with Na-clinoptilolite. Higher thorium uptake was also observed with NaCl-treated zeolite in nitrate media in an earlier study conducted by Misaelides et al. (1995). Although in their research, uranium uptake was not enhanced when a pretreated zeolite sample was used. Baybas and Ulusoy (2011) used composites prepared from polyacrylamide (PAAm) and aluminosilicates for thorium uptake to eliminate the limiting features of aluminosilicates alone, which may be occurring due to aggregation and coagulation in the system. Using a polymer, the diffusion of the ions towards the mineral can be enabled due to the swelling capability of the polymer in the aquatic environment; thus, the adsorption process may be significantly enhanced. As a result, higher adsorption onto the composites of PAAm-Montmorillonite, PAAm-Clinoptilolite, and PAAm-Zeolite was seen compared to aluminosilicates alone. In addition, modification of the samples with phytic acid generated even better results than the composites alone. Nearly 100% thorium adsorption was achieved with phytic acid-treated PAAm-clinoptilolite composite. The pH change results in protonation or deprotonation in the structure of aluminosilicates (Reactions. (19), (20)), causes surface charge and affects overall adsorption efficiency.(19)≡SOH+H+→≡SOH2+(20)≡SOH→SO-+H+
Even though several studies were performed to examine the possible application of sorbents to remove naturally occurring heavy metals and radioactive materials, these studies were primarily performed for decontamination of polluted waters rather than rare earth production. Within that context, Talan and Huang (2021) investigated the removal of thorium and uranium from rare earth elements-containing solutions generated from coarse coal refuse by zeolite adsorption. The best separation performance was achieved while using 2.50 g of 12-µm zeolite sample at a pH value of 3 with a contact period of 2 h. Under these conditions, the adsorption recovery of rare earths, thorium, and uranium into the solid phase was found to be 20.43 wt%, 99.20 wt%, and 89.60 wt%, respectively. Uranium adsorption onto zeolite studied by Kilincarslan and Akyil (2005) suggests similar results concerning contact time. 120 min of contact was identified to be sufficient within the studied range (5–420 mins). Although there are numerous studies on adsorption, it has its disadvantages, such as low selectivity, low loading capacity, complex adsorption behavior, etc. In fact, in Talan and Huang’s (2021) study, it was reported that rare earths and uranium adsorption follow a similar pattern, which creates the separation challenge. The reason for this phenomenon can be the competition between rare earth and uranium ions. As opposed to rare earth elements and uranium, test results indicate that zeolite adsorption is an effective technique for thorium removal. Another explanation for low selectivity towards uranium can be calcium, magnesium, and potassium ions present in the solution. Depending on the ionic strength of the solutions, these cations may cause a displacement, forcing uranium ions into the solution (U.S. EPA,1999).

4. Summary and conclusions

Among all other critical raw materials, rare earths occupy a vast portion. The challenge to meet the demand for rare earth elements will continue rising in the long run, in line with the advancements in fast emerging green technologies and high-tech devices. In that regard, sustainable processing and recycling schemes have presented significant opportunities that align with today’s environmental regulations. This study provided a brief overview of recent advances in rare earth resource exploration activities.
On the other hand, the environmental prospect of rare earth mining needs to be thoroughly considered. Radiation caused by rare earth mining activities raises severe concerns for both the public and the surroundings, and unfortunately, there is not sufficient information on this subject. While focusing on the technical feasibility and economic viability of the rare earth element extraction from conventional and unconventional sources, ensuring that the process is environmentally acceptable is equally crucial. Even though the average concentrations of radioactive matter are lower in the secondary sources than those of the primary sources, it still requires special consideration since their concentrations may be increased along with the processing scheme. This study provided a detailed review of the environmental aspect of rare earth mining and potential separation/remediation techniques for thorium and uranium removal, with the major focus being on separation via precipitation, solvent extraction, and solid-phase extraction due to their wide applications in the field.
Among the techniques reviewed, selective precipitation is easier to operate and less costly; however, a second approach is almost always needed to reduce the radionuclide content further. Typically, a combination of multiple separation techniques is more effective. Solvent extraction is the most effective and preferred technique with proven commercial-scale operations. Various extractant types can be used to separate thorium and uranium in the presence of rare earth-containing solutions under controlled operating conditions. In general, tertiary amines are preferred for uranium separation, while primary amines are more selective towards thorium. However, the use of other types of extractants has also been studied frequently. Ion exchange is used to produce high purity rare earth products, which also has applications in fuel processing. Although the application on a large scale is limited, radionuclide uptake on sorbents with different forms (e.g., microorganisms, an agricultural byproduct, minerals, etc.) is an alternative and promising method, with an advantage over solvent extraction by eliminating the use of a chemical reagent. While some studies showed a separation challenge between rare earth elements and uranium due to their similar adsorption behaviors, other studies achieved high adsorption recoveries using pretreated adsorbents. The application of agricultural byproducts or microorganisms also increases; however, the process is primarily applicable to passive treatment or rare earth recovery from acid mine drainage. Their application in a mining purification process needs to be further investigated.
